1.point: A prayer that declares love for God even while picturing the fire is the chapter's hook; such love is given by God at the stage of adorning, and the chapter will show what God gives the emptied heart and that even love is finally left at the door.
steps: Place the opening quotation and show why it is strange: no trader would say it; the reciter weighs nothing against the fire and still declares love.
Say where such love comes from: the same Munajat says the one praying could not move until God awakened them to His love, so the love is given.

Place that giving on the four-stage road: the first two stages are the traveller's work, the third (adorning) is God's; state what the chapter establishes, including that love carries the traveller until even love is left at the door.

2.point: After the traveller has polished the self and emptied the heart, God adorns the heart with gifts (visions, inspiration, knowledge, light) that no effort can produce; they come in flashes at first and later stay.
steps: Adorning is God's act, not the traveller's; name what comes (visions, inspiration, deeper understanding of the Qur'an).
The traveller's own work only produces a soul able to receive them; the purified soul sees and hears what others cannot.
Scripture confirms that this knowledge and light are given by God, placed in the heart, not won by study.
At first the gifts come as momentary flashes, and there is mercy in that order.
With practice the light stays and becomes the traveller's delight.

3.point: Love is one of these gifts: God places it in the heart by showing something of Himself; because it is given the Imams asked for it in their prayers; it carries the traveller on by emptying the heart further, and it turns worship into the worship of the free.
steps: Love is a gift placed by God in the purified heart, not made by the traveller; it comes when God shows something of His face.
Because it is given, the Imams asked for it; their prayers treat separation from God as worse than punishment.
Love carries the traveller: among fear, renunciation and love, love became the heart and victorious side of mysticism, with fear keeping its place.
Worship that comes from love is the worship of the free, as Imam Ali's three kinds of worship show, with the free worshipping out of love and thanks.
Love is a fire that empties the heart of every preoccupation but remembrance, so it carries forward the clearing the traveller began by effort.

4.point: Love is a means and not the goal; a few stages on the traveller stops attending to his own love and attends to the Beloved only, so even love is left at the door.
steps: Tabatabai: after some stages the traveller sees that love is not the Beloved and gives up love as a possible hindrance, concentrating on the Beloved only.
Why: love is the traveller's own state, so looking at it is still looking at something of one's own; what is left is attention to the love, not the love itself, which cannot be removed.
The same logic already holds for God's gifts: one who seeks God for His gifts is seeking his own self; one who has stopped seeking the gifts can take the same step with his love.
Conclude: at the Beloved only the Beloved remains.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Places the opening quotation and supplies the hook: the reciter pictures the fire and still declares love, which no trader would do. The Mafatih and recitation details could go, but the paragraph does the job of step 1.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Supplies where such love comes from (God awakens the one praying to His love), the link between the hook and the chapter's claim that love is given.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Places the awakening at the third stage, where the work passes to God, and states what the chapter establishes, including the end point (even love left at the door). This is the chapter's thesis statement.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies step 1: adorning is God's act on the soul, not the traveller's, and names the gifts (visions, inspiration, understanding of the Qur'an).

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Supplies step 2: the traveller's work only makes a soul able to receive; Amuli's 'not because they are chosen but because they have furbished their souls' is the hinge between effort and gift. Also introduces the al-An'am verse.

¶6.label: support
¶6.why: Captions the verse (new life, a light to walk by), which is the scriptural evidence for the 'soul that was blind begins to see' claim in ¶5 and is picked up in ¶30 as 'a light to walk by'. Thin: its second sentence only says that many verses say the same.

¶7.label: support
¶7.why: A lead-in to the Yusuf verse that ¶8 reads. It supplies nothing on its own that ¶8 does not state; it exists to set up the quotation.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Supplies step 3: the knowledge given to the muhsinin does not come from books or analysis; God puts it in the heart. This is the clearest statement in the section that the gifts are not made by effort.

¶9.label: aside
¶9.why: The Tehran preacher is a second illustration of ¶8 after the verse has already carried the step, and no later sentence uses him. The second half ('study still matters', Khomeini studied, study and given knowledge reinforce each other) is a qualification the argument never uses. Cutting the paragraph loses nothing the section needs.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Supplies step 4: the gifts come as flashes at first, with Ibn Sina's account and the reason for the order (the light shines from behind clouds while the heart widens).

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Supplies step 5: later the light stays and becomes the traveller's delight; Uways al-Qarani's night of bowing is the instance.

¶12.label: support
¶12.why: Continues the Uways instance: the night felt short, he wished for one long night, which is what 'delight' in ¶11 looks like. The closing remark that the body follows the soul is a new claim the section does not use; borderline with aside.

¶13.label: aside
¶13.why: A caveat (the gifts are not arrival, wonders prove nothing) that the section's point does not need; it serves as a bridge toward Section 4 rather than as a link to this section's point. No later sentence in the section depends on it.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Supplies step 1 of the section: love is a gift placed in the heart by God when He shows something of His face, and it cannot be made by reading; distinguishes this gift from the general gifts of adorning.

¶15.label: support
¶15.why: The two-people comparison makes ¶14 concrete, and 'once given, this love cannot be removed by anyone' is relied on in ¶26. The capacity-of-the-prophets sentence is extra, and the last sentence only introduces the al-Ma'ida verse.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Supplies step 2: because love is given, the Imams asked for it; introduces Du'a Kumayl and its claim that separation is harder than punishment.

¶17.label: support
¶17.why: Glosses the Kumayl quotation (its first sentence repeats ¶16's last), ties the du'a back to the opening Munajat, and introduces a second Imam's prayer, which the plural 'the Imams asked' in the point needs. Partly restating, but the second prayer is used.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: Supplies step 3: love carries the traveller; of fear, renunciation and love, love became the victorious side and heart of mysticism, with fear keeping its place. The Kernel of Kernels sentence is a second source for the same qualification.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Supplies step 4's frame: worship from love is the worship of the free, and Imam Ali names three kinds. Introduces the Nahj al-Balagha quotation.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: Reads the Nahj quotation and supplies the link the step needs: the Nahj text says the free worship in thanks, and the Imam al-Sadiq report adds that they worship because they love Him. The lecture's third reason and Tabatabai's second quotation pile a third and fourth source onto an already-made link.

¶21.label: support
¶21.why: Introduces Rabi'a as the instance of the worship of the free, and her move from fear to love echoes ¶18; ¶22 and ¶29 depend on her being introduced here. The repentance-is-a-gift remark and the legend caveat are extra.

¶22.label: support
¶22.why: The torch and water story is the example of worshipping from love rather than fear of hell or hope of paradise; ¶29 refers back to it ('who carried the torch').

¶23.label: support
¶23.why: One-sentence lead-in to the Lantern of the Path quotation that ¶24 reads.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: Supplies step 5: the fire of love empties the servant of every preoccupation except remembrance, so love carries on the clearing the traveller began by his own effort. This is the mechanism behind 'carries the traveller' and the link back to Section 2.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Supplies step 1 of the section: Tabatabai's account that after a few stages the traveller sees love is not the Beloved and gives it up as a possible hindrance.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: Supplies step 2: why love must be left (it is the traveller's own state) and what is left (attention to one's own love, not the love itself, which ¶15 said no one can remove). Resolves the apparent contradiction.

¶27.label: support
¶27.why: Sa'di's Iyaz story is the example that ¶28 draws its point from ('Mutahhari's point is...'); it is used, not merely placed.

¶28.label: advance
¶28.why: Supplies step 3: the arif does not seek God for His gifts, since then the self would be the real object; a traveller who has made that step with the gifts can make it with his own love. This supplies the 'too' in the section's point. Borderline: ¶25-26 already reach the conclusion, so this is a second route and could be compressed.

¶29.label: aside
¶29.why: A second illustration of ¶28 after the Sa'di story has already served, and the text itself concedes it only 'comes close' to the point. It closes the Rabi'a thread but no later sentence uses it and no step depends on it.

¶30.label: restate
¶30.why: Summarises all three section points (gifts, flashes then stay, love asked for, worship of the free, love left at the door). Every claim has been made already.

¶31.label: aside
¶31.why: Raises a question the chapter does not answer ('what remains of the traveller before God?'); a bridge to the next chapter rather than a link in this section's chain.
